citation: Wagner, P., Branch, W.R., Safari, I. & Chenga, J. 2021. Dendroaspis angusticeps. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2021: e.T13265770A13265778. Accessed on 15 May 2026.

actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This snake occurs widely but sporadically in eastern Africa, from the East African coastal plain in Kenya and Tanzania south through Mozambique to eastern coastal South Africa, and west to Malawi and Zimbabwe (Branch 1998, Spawls et al. 2002, Marais 2004, Broadley and Blaylock 2013). It may occur in southern coastal Somalia, however it is unknown from the Lamu Archipelago and from northern Kenya (Spawls et al. 2002). There are isolated records in Kenya from the Nyambeni Hills, Meru National Park and around Kibwezi, and in forests around Mts. Meru and Kilamanjaro in Tanzania, and around Arusha and Moshi in the same country (Spawls et al. 2002). It is unknown whether these subpopulations are connected, and they may be relicts from a period of higher rainfall and woodland cover (Spawls et al. 2002). This species can occur up to 1,700 m asl in parts of its range, but is mostly found below 500 m asl (Spawls et al. 2002).
documentation.population: This species has been found in high concentrations, especially in coastal Kenya and southeast Tanzania. Concentrations of 2–3 snakes per ha (i.e. 200–300 per km2) have been reported (Spawls et al. 2002).
documentation.habitats: This very fast-moving, diurnal snake inhabits coastal bush and forest, moist savanna and evergreen hill forest, and in agricultural areas including coconut and cashew plantations (Spawls et al. 2002). It is tolerant of some coastal urbanization, and can be found in thick hedges and ornamental trees (Spawls et al. 2002). It can sometimes be found on the ground, but is predominantly arboreal and sleeps in trees in thick patches of branches (Spawls et al. 2002). A clutch of 17 eggs had an incubation period of 2–3 months, and hatchlings have been collected in June and July (Spawls et al. 2002). It feeds mainly on birds and nestlings, rodents and bats, and will take ground-dwelling as well as arboreal species (Spawls et al. 2002).
documentation.threats: Habitat fragmentation in coastal areas (due to urban development) and road mortality may pose localized threats. There is no other information on any threats to this species, however, it is both very widespread and highly adaptable and so it is unlikely to be subject to major threats across its range as a whole. As this is a venomous species it tends to be killed by local people when encountered.
documentation.measures: This species is known from a number of protected areas, including Arusha and Mt Kilimanjaro National Parks in Tanzania, and presumably occurs in others within its wide range. It is unknown whether any other conservation measures are required.
documentation.use_trade: In some areas this species is collected for its venom, which is used for biological research and possibly for anti-venom production. It is found in small numbers in the international pet trade: Jensen et al. (2019) recorded 61 individuals advertised for export from Kenya and Tanzania between 2013 and 2017.
documentation.rationale: This species is considered Least Concern as it has a wide distribution, occurs in several protected areas and is subject to no known threats. However, the taxonomic uncertainty surrounding the species may affect this assessment.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Populations from the southern part of the range (South Africa and southern Mozambique) differ genetically from Tanzanian specimens (Pook et al. 2005). Because Dendroaspis angusticeps was described from specimens collected from KwaZulu-Natal and Maputo (Mozambique), northern populations may require a new specific ranks if genetic differences are found to be at the species level. Some authors informally treated northern populations as Dendroaspis intermedius (see Broadley and Blaylock 2013, Wallach et al. 2014). However, further work is needed within a phylogenetic framework, as is additional sampling that covers the range of both northern and southern populations.
